title: Teaching effectively in a socially distant world
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Writing in summer 2020 as her school prepares for nomadic teaching in year-group bubbles with two-metre distancing, Castelino admits to panic and responds the way she copes best: by writing herself a set of instructions. Her plan covers topic booklets, a trolley of portable resources, a seating plan that lets her reach key students, finely planned explanations and questions, behaviour techniques to prevent low-level disruption without colleagues nearby, and marking done in lessons rather than at home. The piece is a candid, practical teacher's response to constraint, and she hopes the habits will outlast the crisis. It is more craft and routine than curriculum theory, which places it in everyday practice.
points: Booklets for each topic reduce workload, make content consistent and mean absent students already hold the material.
Because the teacher is mobile, a portable bank of resources, such as a trolley with visualiser and mini-whiteboard, becomes part of the teaching plan.
Detailed planning of explanations and checking questions is essential when informal rescue from nearby colleagues is not available.
Preventing low-level disruption through known techniques matters more when removing a student to another room is no longer possible.
Modelling self- and peer-assessment under the visualiser and collecting lined paper replaces carrying books home to mark.
quotes: Yes, it will still take me a while to prepare them well but once made, it will massively reduce my workload, make the presented content more consistent and importantly, if a student misses a lesson, they will already have the material to catch up when they return.

Having a strategic seating plan is something most teachers do anyway. In September, it will be even more important to have students who may need additional support either at the front of the classroom or somewhere where I can speak to them without another student’s head in the way!

From September, however, it is going to be essential to have clear explanations planned to the finest detail. It will also be important to plan how we can explain something if most of the class don’t get it the first time

I will no longer have the support of my Science colleagues being close at hand. Teachers in our school will be surrounded by supportive colleagues but the system of removing a disruptive student to the curriculum leader’s room will no longer be possible. Therefore, it will be very important to avoid disruption, especially of the low-level type.

In terms of checking books, I plan to explicitly model assessing work under the visualiser. For the first few pieces of extended writing questions, I will ask students to answer them on lined paper. Once self- or peer-assessed, I can take these in and check they have done this properly. Doing this will avoid the need to collect books in, transport them in my trolley to a different room and then mark them.

Everything I have described or linked to above are techniques and methods I hope to keep up as much as possible even once this crisis has ended and we return to some form of normal. It could be the push I needed to truly perfect my teaching and ensure my students get the most out of each lesson.
